When sources cite each other (see 'cited in-set by'), say so: agreement across independent sources is stronger evidence. ## Comparative Findings and Benchmarks

Evaluating the hallucination metrics of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) versus long-context models requires rigorous benchmarking frameworks [^crossref:10.1088/2632-2153/ae5442/data1]. However, currently available access to specific source texts presents technical roadblocks such as automated security verification pages, preventing direct extraction of empirical benchmark values from these specific technical repositories [^crossref:10.1088/2632-2153/ae5442/data1, ^crossref:10.36227/techrxiv.177162116.61215374/v1]. Consequently, a granular head-to-head comparison detailing exact error rates, latency trade-offs, and token economics between RAG frameworks and extended-context windows cannot be retrieved from the provided metadata text.

## Open questions

- What specific benchmark suites (e.g., Needle in a Haystack, RGB, or custom hallucination evaluation frameworks) are used to compare RAG and long-context architectures?
- How do long-context models and RAG systems compare empirically on factual hallucination rates when handling multi-document retrieval tasks?
- What would settle them: Full access to peer-reviewed comparative evaluations and structured telemetry datasets comparing retriever-reader pipelines directly against native long-context window models across identical knowledge bases.

## Practical takeaways

- Due to blocked text retrieval across the provided literature portals, no direct production recommendations or tool configurations can be safely validated from these specific sources [^crossref:10.1088/2632-2153/ae5442/data1, ^crossref:10.36227/techrxiv.177162116.61215374/v1].
- What to try first: Verify network and API permissions to ensure automated or manual retrieval scripts bypass anti-bot security challenges before attempting literature synthesis on technical benchmarks [^crossref:10.1088/2632-2153/ae5442/data1].
